label: EXAMPLE POLICY: original illustrative teaching material written for the PhishTriage academic project. Not an institutional policy, legal advice or an official cybersecurity standard.

playbooks.title: Suspected credential theft
playbooks.situation: A message asks the recipient to sign in, verify an account, reset or confirm a password, or restore a mailbox or account that is said to be locked, full, expiring or suspended.
observations: Language asking the reader to log in, verify identity or re-enter a password
Claims that an account or mailbox will be suspended, deactivated or deleted
A link whose visible text names one service while the target host is different
A sender domain that does not belong to the service being named
benign_alternatives: A genuine password-expiry reminder from the organisation's own IT service
A sign-in notification the recipient actually triggered moments earlier
next_steps: Do not use links or forms in the message; open the service by typing its known address
Ask the recipient whether they requested the reset or sign-in
If credentials were entered, escalate to a human responder so the password can be changed and sessions reviewed
limitations: Keyword cues are weak on their own; legitimate IT notices use the same words
This tool cannot see whether the linked page actually collects credentials

playbooks.title: Invoice or payment-detail change
playbooks.situation: A message announces new bank details, asks for an urgent wire transfer, or attaches or links an invoice that requests payment to a changed account.
observations: Words such as new bank details, account number, IBAN, SWIFT, wire transfer or remittance
Pressure to pay today or to keep the request confidential
Reply-To pointing to a different domain from the supplier's usual address
An unexpected invoice attachment
benign_alternatives: A supplier that genuinely changed banks and has announced it through established channels
A routine invoice that matches an existing purchase order
next_steps: Do not change payment details based on the email alone
Verify with the supplier using a phone number or contact already on file, not one given in the message
Involve the finance approver before any transfer, and escalate if money has already been sent
limitations: Payment fraud can come from a genuinely compromised supplier mailbox, so header checks may look normal
The text classifier was not trained specifically on business email compromise

playbooks.title: Sender or Reply-To mismatch
playbooks.situation: The From address, its display name, or the Reply-To address point to different organisations or domains.
observations: Reply-To domain differs from the From domain
The display name contains an email address that differs from the actual From address
A free webmail address used for an organisation's official business
benign_alternatives: Ticketing systems, mailing lists, newsletters and shared mailboxes often set a different Reply-To
Marketing platforms send on behalf of companies from their own domains
next_steps: Compare the addresses with known contacts for that organisation
Do not reply with sensitive information until the sender is confirmed through a separate channel
Treat the mismatch as one signal to weigh with the content, not as proof
limitations: Headers are controlled by the sender and relays; this tool does not authenticate them
A matching From and Reply-To does not prove the sender is genuine

playbooks.title: Suspicious link presentation
playbooks.situation: Links in the message look misleading: the visible text and target differ, or the URL uses an IP address, look-alike or punycode host, embedded credentials, or plain HTTP for a login page.
observations: Visible link text names one domain while the target host is another
Host is an IP address literal or contains punycode (xn--)
User information before an @ sign inside the URL
Plain http:// for something presented as a sign-in or payment page
benign_alternatives: Email marketing and security gateways rewrite links through tracking or scanning domains
Internal tools sometimes use IP addresses on private networks
next_steps: Do not click; inspect the full target address as text
Reach the named service by typing its known address
Escalate to a human reviewer if the link imitates a known brand
limitations: URLs are inspected as strings only; nothing is visited, resolved or reputation-checked
The training data had link targets removed, so the classifier score says nothing about URLs

playbooks.title: Unexpected attachment
playbooks.situation: The message carries or announces an attachment the recipient did not expect, especially archives, executables, scripts, macro-enabled documents or files that ask the reader to enable content.
observations: Attachment metadata showing an archive, script, executable or macro-capable type
A filename with a double extension or a mismatch between name and declared type
Text urging the reader to open the attachment or enable editing or content
benign_alternatives: A colleague sending an expected document, possibly zipped for size
Automated reports that arrive on a known schedule
next_steps: Do not open or extract the attachment
Confirm with the sender through a separate channel that they sent it
Hand the file to people with an isolated analysis environment if further inspection is needed
limitations: Only metadata (name, declared type, size, hash) is recorded; content is never opened or scanned
Declared types and filenames can be falsified by the sender

playbooks.title: Legitimate urgent communication
playbooks.situation: A message is urgent or asks for action but may well be genuine, for example a real deadline, outage notice, schedule change or security announcement from a known source.
observations: Urgency without requests for credentials, payment changes or unexpected attachments
Content consistent with work the recipient is already doing
Links, if any, point to the organisation's usual domains
benign_alternatives: This playbook itself describes the benign case: urgency alone is common in genuine mail
next_steps: Act through normal channels, such as opening the known portal rather than the email link, when unsure
Avoid over-escalating: record why the message appears legitimate
Re-check if a follow-up message adds credential, payment or attachment requests
limitations: Attackers deliberately imitate genuine urgent notices
A legitimate-looking message can still come from a compromised account

playbooks.title: Missing or conflicting evidence
playbooks.situation: Important information is unavailable (no headers, pasted text only, truncated content), checks failed, or the available signals disagree with each other.
observations: Evidence marked unavailable or error
Authentication-Results claims that disagree with each other
Classifier output that conflicts with header or link observations
Input truncated by the length policy
benign_alternatives: Missing headers are normal for pasted text and do not imply danger
next_steps: State explicitly what is missing; do not treat missing information as evidence of safety
Ask for the original message as an .eml file if headers or attachments matter
Prefer a cautious, human-reviewed outcome over a confident automated verdict
limitations: No automated tool can fill in information that was never provided

playbooks.title: Human escalation and verification
playbooks.situation: A case needs a human decision: high-impact requests (money, credentials, sensitive data), signs that the recipient already acted, conflicting evidence, or low confidence in the automated triage.
observations: The recipient may have clicked, replied, paid or entered credentials
Requests involving money, credentials or personal data
Strong disagreement between evidence sources
benign_alternatives: Escalation is a safe default and does not imply the message is malicious
next_steps: Hand over the case summary with evidence IDs and their status (observed, unverified claim, unavailable, error)
Verify with the purported sender using contact details already on file
If someone already acted, prioritise containment steps such as password changes and payment recall through the proper people
limitations: This example playbook does not define who the responders are in any real organisation
Timelines and contacts must come from the actual organisation's own procedures
